{{Short description|Statistical regression analysis with long list of variables}}
{{citations|date=January 2021}}
[[Pejorative]]ly, a '''kitchen sink regression''' is a statistical [[regression analysis|regression]]  which uses a long list of possible [[independent variable]]s to attempt to explain [[variance]] in a [[dependent variable]]. In [[economics]], [[psychology]], and other [[social sciences]], regression analysis is typically used [[deductive reasoning|deductively]] to test hypotheses, but a kitchen sink regression does not follow this norm. Instead, the analyst throws "[[wikt:everything but the kitchen sink|everything but the kitchen sink]]" into the regression in hopes of finding some statistical pattern.{{citation needed|date=August 2015}}

This type of regression often leads to [[overfitting]] (i.e. misleadingly suggesting relationships between independent and dependent variables in the data, which can lead to [[hasty generalization]]s). The reason for this is that the more independent variables are included in a regression, the greater the probability that one or more will be found to be [[statistical significance|statistically significant]] while in fact having no causal effect on the dependent variable as an implication of the definition of [[confidence intervals]]&mdash;that is, the more likely the results are to be afflicted with [[Type I error]].
